subject: Operating Systems
exam_relevance: 8-10 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Oracle is a Database Management System (DBMS), not an OS. Linux and Windows are operating systems. (BPSC TRE 2.0 actual question)

questions.question: The software that runs on hardware and serves as a platform for other software is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: An OS is system software that manages hardware resources and provides a platform for application software. (BPSC TRE 2.0)

questions.question: Which technique marks the beginning of computer communications by allowing multiple users to use a computer simultaneously?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Time Sharing OS allows multiple users to share CPU time simultaneously, marking the start of computer communications. (BPSC TRE 1.0)

questions.question: In a Batch Operating System, jobs are:

options.A: Processed one by one without user interaction
options.B: Processed in real time with strict deadlines
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Batch OS groups similar jobs and processes them without user interaction. No real-time interaction occurs.

questions.question: A Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) is used in:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RTOS is used wherever strict time constraints exist: air traffic control, missile systems, and medical equipment all qualify.

questions.question: Which is NOT a system tool among the following?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Folder is a file system concept, not a system tool. Scandisk and Defragmenter are system maintenance tools. (BPSC TRE 2.0)

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of an Operating System?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: OS handles memory management, process management, and file system management — all three are core OS functions.

questions.question: A Distributed Operating System manages:

options.A: Multiple computers connected via a network as a single system
options.B: A single processor with multiple cores
options.C: Multiple processors on a single machine
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Distributed OS manages multiple independent computers connected via network, presenting them as a single unified system.

questions.question: Which OS type is best suited for applications requiring guaranteed response within a fixed time limit?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Real-Time OS guarantees that critical tasks complete within fixed deadlines, essential for safety-critical applications.

questions.question: The kernel is:

options.B: The core part of the operating system
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The kernel is the core of the OS that manages hardware resources, process scheduling, and system calls.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid process state in an operating system?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three — Ready, Running, and Waiting — are valid process states. The five states are: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated.

questions.question: The Process Control Block (PCB) stores:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: PCB stores PID, state, program counter, CPU registers, memory info, I/O status — all three options are part of PCB.

questions.question: When a running process requests an I/O operation, it moves to the _____ state:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: When a process requests I/O, it cannot continue CPU execution and moves to Waiting/Blocked state until I/O completes.

questions.question: The Program Counter (PC) in a PCB stores:

options.A: The total memory used by the process
options.B: The address of the next instruction to be executed
options.C: The number of instructions executed so far
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Program Counter stores the address of the next instruction to execute, allowing the process to resume after a context switch.

questions.question: A process moves from the New state to the Ready state when:

options.A: The CPU scheduler assigns it the CPU
options.B: It is admitted by the OS and loaded into memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A new process is admitted (loaded into main memory) and placed in the Ready queue; it then transitions to the Ready state.

questions.question: Context switching refers to:

options.A: Saving the state of the current process and loading the state of the next process
options.B: Terminating one process and starting another
options.C: Switching between user mode and kernel mode
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Context switch saves PCB of current process and loads PCB of next scheduled process, allowing CPU to switch between processes.

questions.question: Which component of the PCB stores the values of all CPU registers at the time of a context switch?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CPU register save area in PCB stores all register values (accumulators, index registers, etc.) so process can resume correctly.

questions.question: A process is in the Running state means:

options.A: It is waiting for I/O completion
options.B: It is ready to execute but waiting for the CPU
options.C: It is currently executing on the CPU
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Running state means the process is currently being executed by the CPU. Only one process runs per CPU at any instant.

questions.question: The scheduler that selects a process from the ready queue to give CPU is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Short-term scheduler (CPU scheduler) selects which ready process gets the CPU next. It runs very frequently (milliseconds).

questions.question: Dispatch latency is the time taken by the dispatcher to:

options.A: Stop one process and start another on the CPU
options.C: Load a new process from disk to memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Dispatch latency = time for dispatcher to stop current process, perform context switch, and start the next process.

questions.question: In FCFS (First Come First Served) scheduling, processes are served in the order they:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: FCFS is non-preemptive and serves processes in arrival order. It is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm.

questions.question: The Convoy Effect in FCFS scheduling occurs when:

options.B: Short processes are stuck waiting behind a long CPU-bound process
options.C: High-priority processes wait for low-priority processes
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Convoy effect: short processes wait behind one long process in FCFS, causing all CPU and I/O devices to wait — reduces utilization.

questions.question: SJF (Shortest Job First) scheduling is optimal in terms of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SJF is proven optimal for minimizing average waiting time among all non-preemptive algorithms. But it may cause starvation.

questions.question: SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) is the preemptive version of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SRTF is preemptive SJF: a new process with shorter remaining time preempts the current running process.

questions.question: In Round Robin scheduling, the time quantum (time slice) determines:

options.C: How long each process runs before being preempted
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RR gives each process a fixed time slice (quantum). After quantum expires, the process is preempted and placed at end of queue.

questions.question: In Priority Scheduling, starvation can occur because:

options.A: All processes have the same priority
options.B: Low-priority jobs wait indefinitely for CPU
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Starvation: low-priority processes wait indefinitely as high-priority processes continuously arrive. Solution: aging (increase priority over time).

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm is preemptive by nature?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Round Robin is inherently preemptive — each process runs for a time quantum then is preempted. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF run to completion.

questions.question: If processes P1, P2, P3 arrive at time 0 with burst times 24, 3, 3 respectively using FCFS, the average waiting time is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: P1 waits 0, P2 waits 24, P3 waits 27. Avg WT = (0+24+27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms. Classic Silberschatz example.

questions.question: For the same processes P1(BT=24), P2(BT=3), P3(BT=3) using SJF, the average waiting time is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SJF order: P2(0→3), P3(3→6), P1(6→30). WT: P2=0, P3=3, P1=6. Avg=(0+3+6)/3=3 ms. SJF optimal for avg waiting time.

questions.question: Turnaround time for a process is defined as:

options.A: Time from submission to completion of the process
options.B: Time the process spends waiting in the ready queue
options.C: Time the process spends on the CPU
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Turnaround Time = Completion Time − Arrival Time = Burst Time + Waiting Time.

questions.question: Aging is a technique used in scheduling to:

options.A: Gradually increase the priority of processes that have waited long
options.B: Reduce the time quantum for long-running processes
options.C: Terminate processes that have been running too long
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Aging prevents starvation by gradually increasing the priority of waiting processes so they eventually get CPU time.

questions.question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm is best for interactive systems?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Round Robin is best for time-sharing/interactive systems as it gives each process a fair share of CPU time (small time quantum).

questions.question: If the time quantum in Round Robin is very large, it behaves like:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: With a very large time quantum, each process runs to completion before the next starts — identical to FCFS behavior.

questions.question: CPU utilization and throughput are measures of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CPU utilization (% time CPU is busy) and throughput (processes completed per unit time) are CPU scheduling performance metrics.

questions.question: In Multilevel Queue Scheduling, which queue gets the HIGHEST priority?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In multilevel queue: System processes > Interactive processes > Background processes. System processes have highest priority.

questions.question: The four necessary conditions for deadlock are:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Deadlock requires ALL four: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. A and B are both correct — D applies.

questions.question: Mutual Exclusion as a deadlock condition means:

options.A: Processes must hold resources while waiting for more
options.B: At least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode
options.C: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Mutual Exclusion: at least one resource is non-sharable — only one process at a time can use it.

questions.question: The Banker's Algorithm is used for:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Banker's Algorithm (Dijkstra) is a deadlock AVOIDANCE algorithm. It checks if granting a resource keeps the system in a safe state.

questions.question: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive that can be used to:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Semaphores solve critical section problems, control shared resource access, and implement mutual exclusion — all three are correct.

questions.question: A binary semaphore can take values:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Binary semaphore: values restricted to 0 or 1. Used for mutual exclusion (like a mutex). Counting semaphore takes 0 to N.

questions.question: The critical section problem requires which properties to be satisfied?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Critical section solution must satisfy all three: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting (Silberschatz Chapter 6).

questions.question: Circular Wait as a deadlock condition means:

options.A: All processes are in a circular CPU queue
options.B: Processes form a ring topology in a network
options.C: A set of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next process in the set
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Circular Wait: P1 waits for resource held by P2, P2 waits for resource held by P3, ... Pn waits for resource held by P1.

questions.question: To prevent deadlock, which condition can be eliminated by enforcing a total ordering on resource types?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Circular Wait is eliminated by assigning a total order to resource types and requiring processes to request resources in that order.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait are all 4 necessary conditions. Hence none of A/B/C is excluded.

questions.question: The wait() (P) operation on a semaphore S performs:

options.A: Increments S and wakes a blocked process if any
options.B: Resets S to its initial value
options.C: Decrements S; if S < 0, the process blocks
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: wait(S)/P(S): S--; if S<0, block the process. signal(S)/V(S): S++; if S<=0, wake a blocked process.

questions.question: Which deadlock handling approach checks the state before allocating resources?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Deadlock Avoidance (e.g., Banker's Algorithm) checks system state before each allocation to ensure a safe state is maintained.

questions.question: Race condition occurs when:

options.A: A process runs faster than another
options.B: Concurrent access to shared data causes race
options.C: Two processes compete for CPU time
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Race condition: outcome depends on process execution order. Solved by synchronization mechanisms like mutex and semaphores.

questions.question: Which memory management technique is used to shift processes to make all free memory contiguous (in one block)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Compaction: relocates processes to consolidate all free memory into one large block, eliminating external fragmentation. (BPSC TRE 1.0)

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a memory management technique?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Fragmentation is a problem/side-effect, not a technique. Paging and Segmentation are memory management techniques. (BPSC TRE 3.0)

questions.question: In Paging, a page is:

options.A: A variable-size block of physical memory
options.B: A named segment of a program
options.C: A fixed-size block of virtual (logical) memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In paging, logical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called pages; physical memory is divided into frames of same size. (BPSC TRE 3.0)

questions.question: If page size is 4 KB, the number of bits required for the page offset is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 4 KB = 4096 = 2^12 bytes, so page offset needs 12 bits to address any byte within a page. (BPSC TRE 3.0)

questions.question: If physical memory is 6 GB and virtual address space is 10 GB, the amount of data that must be swapped out is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual - Physical = 10 - 6 = 4 GB must reside on disk (swap space) at any time when fully loaded. (BPSC TRE 3.0)

questions.question: Internal fragmentation occurs in:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Internal fragmentation (wasted space inside allocated block) occurs in both Paging and Fixed-size partitioning, not Segmentation.

questions.question: External fragmentation occurs in:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: External fragmentation (free memory in non-contiguous blocks) occurs in Segmentation and variable partitioning, not Paging.

questions.question: The page table in paging is used to:

options.A: Store the contents of each page
options.B: Map logical page numbers to physical frame numbers
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Page table maps each logical page number to the corresponding physical frame number for address translation.

questions.question: In a system with 32-bit logical address and 4 KB page size, the number of entries in the page table is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Page offset = 12 bits (4KB=2^12), page number = 32-12 = 20 bits, so page table entries = 2^20 = 1M entries.

questions.question: In segmentation, the logical address consists of:

options.C: Segment number and offset within the segment
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Segmentation logical address = <segment number, offset>. Each segment has a base and limit in the segment table.

questions.question: Which memory allocation strategy selects the smallest hole that is large enough to accommodate the process?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Best Fit: allocates the smallest sufficient hole. Minimizes wasted space in the allocated hole but can leave tiny unusable fragments.

questions.question: Swapping in memory management refers to:

options.A: Replacing one page with another in main memory
options.B: Exchanging two processes between ready queue and running state
options.C: Moving an entire process from main memory to disk and back
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Swapping: entire process moved to backing store (disk) when memory is needed, then swapped back in for execution.

questions.question: In FIFO page replacement, which page is replaced when a page fault occurs?

options.A: The page that has been in memory the longest (oldest)
options.C: The page that will not be used for the longest time
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: FIFO replaces the oldest page (the one that entered memory first), maintaining a simple queue of pages.

questions.question: Belady's Anomaly refers to the phenomenon where:

options.A: Increasing the number of page frames increases the number of page faults in FIFO
options.B: LRU gives worse performance than FIFO
options.C: More processes cause fewer page faults
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Belady's Anomaly: in FIFO, more frames can paradoxically cause more page faults. LRU and Optimal do not suffer from this anomaly.

questions.question: The Optimal Page Replacement algorithm replaces:

options.A: Page not used for longest future time
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Optimal (OPT/MIN) replaces the page that won't be needed for the longest future time — theoretically optimal but needs future knowledge.

questions.question: LRU (Least Recently Used) page replacement replaces:

options.A: The page with the lowest page number
options.B: The page that was used least recently (longest time ago)
options.C: The page that was loaded most recently
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LRU replaces the page that was used least recently, based on the principle of temporal locality.

questions.question: Thrashing in an operating system refers to:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Thrashing: excessive page faults cause the system to spend more time swapping pages than executing processes — CPU utilization drops drastically.

questions.question: Which page replacement algorithm does NOT suffer from Belady's Anomaly?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms — they never suffer Belady's Anomaly. FIFO and Clock are not stack algorithms.

questions.question: For the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2 with 3 frames using FIFO, number of page faults is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Classic Silberschatz example: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2 with 3 frames FIFO gives 9 page faults (3 compulsory + 6 replacement).

questions.question: The working set model in virtual memory is used to:

options.B: Track pages actively used by a process
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Working Set Model tracks the set of pages a process actively references in a time window to prevent thrashing.

questions.question: A page fault occurs when:

options.A: The CPU tries to execute an illegal instruction
options.B: A referenced page is not in main memory (not in any frame)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Page fault: page referenced by process is not in physical memory — OS must load it from disk into a free or replaced frame.

questions.question: Among FIFO, LRU, and Optimal page replacement algorithms, which gives the minimum number of page faults?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Optimal gives the minimum possible page faults (theoretical upper bound). It needs future reference knowledge, so not implementable.

questions.question: TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is typically organized as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: TLB is an associative/content-addressable cache that searches all entries simultaneously for fast page table lookups. (BPSC TRE 3.0)

questions.question: Virtual memory allows:

options.A: Programs larger than physical memory to run
options.B: More processes to run concurrently than physical memory would allow
options.C: Processes to be isolated from each other's memory space
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual memory provides all three benefits: running programs larger than RAM, more multiprogramming, and process isolation.

questions.question: The effective memory access time (EMAT) with TLB is calculated using:

options.B: CPU clock speed and memory bus width
options.C: TLB hit ratio, TLB access time, and memory access time
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: EMAT = (hit ratio × (TLB time + mem time)) + ((1-hit ratio) × (TLB time + 2×mem time)). All three factors in A are needed.

questions.question: Swap space in virtual memory is located on:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Swap space (backing store) is a reserved area on the hard disk used to hold pages not currently in physical memory.

questions.question: When the TLB misses (page number not found in TLB), the OS:

options.B: Looks up the page table in main memory to find the frame number
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: TLB miss: access main memory page table to get frame number, then update TLB with this mapping (unless page is also absent → page fault).

questions.question: Demand paging means:

options.A: All pages of a process are loaded before execution begins
options.B: Pages are prefetched based on prediction
options.C: Pages are loaded into memory only when they are needed (on page fault)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Demand paging: pages brought into memory only on demand (when page fault occurs), reducing initial load time and memory use.

questions.question: The valid-invalid bit in a page table entry indicates:

options.A: Whether the page can be executed
options.B: Whether page is in RAM or on disk
options.C: Whether the page has been modified
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Valid bit=1: page is in physical memory. Valid bit=0: page is on disk — accessing it triggers a page fault.

questions.question: If physical memory is 64 GB and page size is 4 KB, the number of bits for the physical frame number is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 64 GB = 2^36 bytes; page size = 4 KB = 2^12. Frames = 2^36/2^12 = 2^24. So frame number needs 24 bits.

questions.question: With disk head at cylinder 53, service request queue 98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67 using FCFS disk scheduling, the total head movement is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) disk scheduling selects the request:

options.B: Closest to the current head position
options.C: That arrived first in the queue
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SSTF always services the request nearest to the current head position, minimizing seek time but potentially causing starvation.

questions.question: In SCAN (elevator) disk scheduling, the disk head:

options.A: Moves in one direction servicing requests, reaches end, then reverses
options.B: Always moves from innermost to outermost cylinder
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SCAN (elevator): head moves in one direction, services all requests, then reverses — like an elevator. Avoids starvation unlike SSTF.

questions.question: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) differs from SCAN in that:

options.A: It services requests in circular order regardless of head position
options.B: It reverses direction after servicing each request
options.C: At the end, head jumps back to start without servicing on the return trip
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: C-SCAN: head sweeps in one direction; at end, jumps back to start without servicing — provides more uniform wait times than SCAN.

questions.question: Which disk scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of requests at the edges of the disk?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SSTF can cause starvation: if requests keep arriving near current head position, distant requests wait indefinitely.

questions.question: The seek time in disk I/O is the time for:

options.A: Transferring data from disk to memory
options.B: Waiting for the desired sector to rotate under the head
options.C: Moving the disk arm to the correct cylinder (track)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Seek time: arm movement to correct track. Rotational latency: waiting for sector. Transfer time: actual data transfer.

questions.question: Total disk access time = :

options.A: Seek time + Rotational latency + Transfer time
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Total disk access time = Seek Time (arm to track) + Rotational Latency (wait for sector) + Transfer Time (data read/write).

questions.question: FCFS disk scheduling is:

options.B: Fair to all requests but can have high total head movement
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: FCFS is fair (no starvation) but can have high total head movement as it doesn't optimize for seek distance.

questions.question: A compiler translates:

options.A: High-level language line by line during execution
options.C: High-level language to machine code (all at once)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Compiler translates entire high-level language program to machine code at once before execution. Interpreter translates line by line.

questions.question: An assembler converts:

options.C: Assembly language (mnemonic code) to machine language (binary)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Assembler: assembly language (mnemonics like MOV, ADD) → machine language (binary opcodes). One-to-one translation.

questions.question: The difference between a compiler and an interpreter is:

options.A: Compiler translates entire program at once; interpreter translates one statement at a time
options.B: Compiler is faster during execution; interpreter is slower
options.C: Interpreter produces an executable file; compiler does not
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Both A and B are correct: compiler translates all at once (faster execution); interpreter line-by-line (slower execution). D applies.

questions.question: A linker is responsible for:

options.A: Combining multiple object files and libraries into a single executable
options.B: Loading the executable into memory for execution
options.C: Converting source code into object code
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Linker: combines compiled object files (.obj) and library files into a single executable file, resolving external references.

questions.question: A loader is responsible for:

options.A: Translating source code to object code
options.B: Loading the executable program from disk into main memory for execution
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Loader: loads the executable file from secondary storage into RAM and prepares it for CPU execution.

questions.question: Method of accessing I/O by repeatedly checking the status of an I/O device is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Polling: CPU repeatedly checks I/O device status in a busy-wait loop. Wasteful of CPU time. Also called program-controlled I/O. (BPSC TRE 1.0)

questions.question: In Interrupt-Driven I/O, the CPU:

options.A: Directly accesses memory without CPU involvement
options.B: Continuously polls the device until I/O completes
options.C: Initiates I/O then continues other work; device interrupts CPU when done
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Interrupt-driven I/O: CPU starts I/O, continues other tasks, device sends interrupt when done — more efficient than polling.

questions.question: DMA (Direct Memory Access) is used to:

options.A: Transfer data directly between I/O devices and memory without CPU involvement
options.B: Replace the need for a memory controller
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DMA controller transfers data between I/O devices and RAM directly, freeing CPU for other tasks during large data transfers.

questions.question: The Dining Philosophers problem illustrates:

options.A: Deadlock and starvation in concurrent systems
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Dining Philosophers: 5 philosophers, 5 chopsticks — classic problem illustrating deadlock and starvation in resource allocation.

questions.question: The Reader-Writer problem addresses:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Reader-Writer: multiple readers can read simultaneously, but writers need exclusive access. Requires synchronization to prevent inconsistency.

questions.question: Peterson's solution solves the critical section problem for:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Peterson's solution is a software-based solution for the critical section problem for exactly two processes.

questions.question: A process and a thread differ in that:

options.A: Threads share the same address space within a process; processes have separate address spaces
options.B: Processes are faster to create than threads
options.C: Threads are heavier than processes in terms of resource consumption
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Threads share code, data, and OS resources of their parent process. Processes are independent with separate address spaces.

questions.question: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) is used for:

options.C: Buffering slow I/O output onto disk
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Spooling: output for slow devices (printers) is written to disk spool queue, allowing CPU to continue while printer works at its own pace.

questions.question: A monolithic kernel, as used in Linux, means:

options.A: The kernel runs in user space
options.B: Each OS service runs in a separate process
options.C: All OS services run in kernel space (single large executable)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Monolithic kernel: all OS services (file system, drivers, scheduler) run in kernel space as one unit. Efficient but less modular.

questions.question: The Producer-Consumer problem is solved using semaphores where:

options.A: Mutex ensures mutual exclusion on the buffer
options.B: Full semaphore tracks filled slots; Empty semaphore tracks empty slots
options.C: Both mutex and counting semaphores are used together
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Producer-Consumer uses: Empty (count empty slots), Full (count filled slots) counting semaphores + mutex for exclusive buffer access. All three correct.
